course.title: Russian Culture & Civilization
course.description: A respectful tour across the largest country on Earth: its vast geography, a thousand years of history from Kievan Rus to modern Russia, the Cyrillic language, and the literature, music, ballet, visual arts, faith, and daily life that grew there. Topic coverage and structure are adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). All prose here is original, and names are romanized.

questions.prompt: By total land area, Russia ranks as the world's...
questions.explanation: At about 17 million square kilometers, Russia is the largest country by area, spanning eleven time zones - see 'Geography and the vast expanse'.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range is the traditional divide between European and Asian Russia?
questions.explanation: The Ural Mountains run north to south and mark the conventional boundary between Europe and Asia.

questions.prompt: Kievan Rus adopted Orthodox Christianity under Vladimir the Great in the year...
questions.explanation: The conversion of 988 tied the early East Slavic state to Byzantine Christianity and culture.

questions.prompt: Russian is written using which alphabet?
questions.explanation: The Cyrillic alphabet, traced to Saints Cyril and Methodius, is used for Russian - see 'The Russian language and Cyrillic'.

questions.prompt: The novels 'War and Peace' and 'Anna Karenina' were written by...
questions.explanation: Leo Tolstoy (1828-1910) wrote both monumental novels.

questions.prompt: The ballets 'Swan Lake' and 'The Nutcracker' were composed by...
questions.explanation: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840-1893) composed both, along with 'The Sleeping Beauty'.

questions.prompt: The revolution that brought the Bolsheviks to power happened in...
questions.explanation: The 1917 October Revolution, led by Lenin's Bolsheviks, followed the February abdication of the last tsar.

questions.prompt: The Soviet Union was formally dissolved in...
questions.explanation: The USSR broke apart at the end of 1991, and the modern Russian Federation emerged.

lessons.title: Geography and the vast expanse
lessons.grammar_note: Say 'Siberia' for the Asian interior east of the Urals; it is a region, not a separate country.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe just how large Russia is, locate its major regions, and name the natural features that shape the country. By the end you will be able to explain why one nation can stretch across eleven time zones yet still feel bound together by rivers, railways, and a single capital. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which mountain range is the traditional divide between European and Asian Russia? Hold that answer in mind as we travel east from Moscow toward the Pacific coast. You will also be ready to picture the sharp contrast between the crowded western heartland, where most people live, and the thinly settled wilderness of Siberia that covers the bulk of the land. Finally, you will understand how distance itself became a theme in Russian life, so much so that the long winter, the open plain, and the endless road recur again and again in the country's songs, novels, and sense of self.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Russia covers roughly 17 million square kilometers, making it the largest country on Earth, nearly twice the size of the next-largest. It reaches from the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad in the west to the Bering Strait in the east, and from the Arctic Ocean down to the Caucasus and the steppes of the south. The Ural Mountains, a low worn range running north to south, form the conventional border between European Russia and Asian Russia. West of the Urals lies the densely populated heartland around Moscow and Saint Petersburg; east of them stretches Siberia, a cold immensity of taiga forest, tundra, and frozen river basins. The climate is mostly continental, with short warm summers and long hard winters. Great rivers such as the Volga, the longest in Europe, and the Ob, Yenisei, and Lena of Siberia organize settlement and trade. Because the land is so wide, time, transport, and sheer distance have always been central facts of Russian life and politics.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Several landmarks capture the scale of the country. Lake Baikal in southern Siberia is the deepest and oldest freshwater lake in the world, holding a huge share of the planet's unfrozen fresh water. Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, at about 5,642 meters, is the highest peak in Europe. The Volga River, around 3,530 kilometers long, has been called Mother Volga for its role in Russian trade, folklore, and song. The Trans-Siberian Railway, completed in the early twentieth century, runs more than 9,000 kilometers from Moscow to Vladivostok on the Pacific, the longest single rail line on Earth and a feat that stitched the far east to the center. Moscow, the capital, grew up around the fortified Kremlin on the Moskva River, while Saint Petersburg, built on marshland at the Baltic, became the imperial 'window on the West.' Together these places map a country defined by extremes of cold, distance, and water.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) About how many square kilometers does Russia cover, and what is its world rank by area? 2) Which range divides European from Asian Russia? 3) Name the deepest lake in the world, found in Siberia. 4) Which river is the longest in Europe and a symbol of Russian trade? 5) How many time zones does the country span? 6) What is the eastern terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway? Answers: 1) About 17 million square kilometers; the largest country on Earth. 2) The Ural Mountains. 3) Lake Baikal. 4) The Volga. 5) Eleven. 6) Vladivostok, on the Pacific coast.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling Siberia a separate country; it is a vast region of Russia east of the Urals, not an independent state. Mistake: imagining Russia is uniformly frozen; the south has warm steppe and a short growing season, and summers in the heartland can be hot. Mistake: confusing Moscow and Saint Petersburg; Moscow is the inland capital around the Kremlin, while Saint Petersburg is the Baltic port founded to face Europe. Exit: (a) Which mountains mark the Europe-Asia divide within Russia? (b) Which Siberian lake holds the most fresh water of any lake on Earth? (c) Which city is the current capital? Answers: the Ural Mountains; Lake Baikal; Moscow. Keep the sheer size of the country in mind, because it shapes nearly every chapter of the history that follows.

lessons.title: History I: Kievan Rus, the Mongol yoke, and the Tsars
lessons.grammar_note: Use 'tsar' (also spelled czar) for the Russian monarch; the word descends from the Roman title Caesar.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace the Russian state from its origins among the East Slavs to the rise of a mighty empire. By the end you will be able to place four turning points in order: the founding of Kievan Rus, the conversion to Orthodox Christianity, the long domination by the Mongols, and the gathering of power by Moscow under the tsars. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, in what year did Vladimir the Great adopt Christianity for his realm? You will learn to tell apart three famous rulers often confused: Ivan the Terrible, who first took the title tsar; Peter the Great, who turned the country toward Europe; and Catherine the Great, who expanded it further. You will also see how a small principality around Moscow grew, over centuries, into one of the largest empires in human history, and why Orthodoxy, autocracy, and territory became its lasting pillars.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The first East Slavic state, Kievan Rus, took shape in the late ninth century, traditionally dated to around 882 when the ruler Oleg made Kiev his center. The dynasty traced itself to the Varangian prince Rurik. In 988 Vladimir the Great accepted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium, binding the Rus to Greek faith, letters, and art. In the thirteenth century the Mongols swept in, sacking Kiev in 1240; for roughly two and a half centuries the Russian principalities paid tribute to the Golden Horde, a period later called the Mongol or Tatar yoke. During these years Moscow slowly rose as the strongest principality. Ivan III, called the Great, threw off Mongol overlordship by 1480. His grandson Ivan IV, the Terrible, was crowned the first tsar of all Russia in 1547. After a chaotic Time of Troubles, the Romanov dynasty began in 1613 and would rule until 1917.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Ivan IV, the Terrible, reigned from 1547 to 1584; he centralized power, expanded east into Siberia, and earned his fearsome name through violent purges late in his rule. Peter the Great, reigning from 1682 to 1725, is remembered for dragging Russia toward western Europe: he modernized the army, built a navy, reformed government, founded the new capital of Saint Petersburg in 1703, and proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721. Catherine the Great, a German-born princess who ruled from 1762 to 1796, extended the empire's borders to the Black Sea and into Poland, corresponded with Enlightenment thinkers, and expanded the arts and education, even as serfdom tightened for the peasantry. Other milestones include the Romanov accession of Michael in 1613 and the earlier reign of Ivan III, the Great. Together these rulers built the autocratic, Orthodox, and ever-expanding state that defined imperial Russia.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What was the first East Slavic state, and roughly when did it form? 2) In what year did Vladimir the Great convert to Orthodox Christianity? 3) What name is given to the long period of Mongol domination? 4) Who was crowned the first tsar of all Russia, and in what year? 5) Which ruler founded Saint Petersburg, and when? 6) Which empress expanded Russia to the Black Sea in the late eighteenth century? Answers: 1) Kievan Rus, around 882. 2) 988. 3) The Mongol, or Tatar, yoke. 4) Ivan IV, the Terrible, in 1547. 5) Peter the Great, in 1703. 6) Catherine the Great.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the three great rulers; Ivan the Terrible first took the title tsar, Peter the Great westernized and founded Saint Petersburg, and Catherine the Great expanded the empire southward. Mistake: thinking the Mongols ruled Russia directly; the princes mostly kept their thrones but paid heavy tribute to the Golden Horde. Mistake: dating the Romanovs too early; their dynasty began in 1613, after the Time of Troubles. Exit: (a) Which ruler founded Saint Petersburg and in what year? (b) When did Vladimir the Great adopt Christianity? (c) Who was the first tsar of all Russia? Answers: Peter the Great, 1703; 988; Ivan IV, the Terrible. Next we carry the story from a glittering empire into revolution and the Soviet century.

lessons.title: History II: Revolution, the Soviet era, and post-1991 Russia
lessons.grammar_note: The USSR, or Soviet Union, was the federal state that existed from 1922 to 1991; 'Russia' is both the former core republic and the successor state.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Follow Russia from the fall of the monarchy through seven decades of Soviet rule and into the present. By the end you will be able to place the key dates in order: the 1917 revolutions, the forming of the Soviet Union, the ordeal of the Second World War, the Cold War space race, and the collapse of 1991. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, in what year was the Soviet Union dissolved? You will learn why 1917 marks one of the most consequential turning points of the twentieth century, how the Soviet state industrialized at enormous human cost, and how the superpower rivalry shaped the world. You will also see why the years after 1991 brought painful economic change along with a reopening of Russian cultural and religious life, setting the stage for the modern Russian Federation that exists today.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: By the early twentieth century, defeat in war and deep inequality strained the empire. In February 1917 Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, ending Romanov rule; in October 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power. A brutal civil war followed from 1918 to 1922, after which the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was founded in 1922. Under Joseph Stalin the state forced rapid industrialization and collectivized farming, policies that brought famine, mass repression, and the purges of the late 1930s. In 1941 Nazi Germany invaded, launching what Russians call the Great Patriotic War; the Soviet Union suffered staggering losses before victory in 1945. The postwar decades brought the Cold War with the United States, early triumphs in space, and slow stagnation. Reforms under Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s could not hold the union together, and the USSR dissolved at the end of 1991, leaving the Russian Federation as its largest successor.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Vladimir Lenin led the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 and headed the new state until his death in 1924. Joseph Stalin then ruled until 1953, overseeing forced industrialization, collectivization, and the terror of the purges, but also the wartime victory over Germany. The Soviet space program produced historic firsts: Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957, and Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, in 1961. Nikita Khrushchev and later Leonid Brezhnev led through the long Cold War standoff. Mikhail Gorbachev, taking power in 1985, introduced perestroika, a restructuring of the economy, and glasnost, a new openness, hoping to save the system. Instead the union unraveled, and Boris Yeltsin became the first president of an independent Russia in 1991. These figures and events frame the century that transformed Russia from empire to superpower and then to a struggling new republic.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What happened to Tsar Nicholas II in February 1917? 2) Who led the Bolsheviks in the October Revolution? 3) When was the Soviet Union founded? 4) What do Russians call the Second World War against Germany? 5) Who became the first human in space, and in what year? 6) In what year did the USSR dissolve, and who became Russia's first president? Answers: 1) He abdicated, ending Romanov rule. 2) Vladimir Lenin. 3) 1922. 4) The Great Patriotic War. 5) Yuri Gagarin, in 1961. 6) 1991; Boris Yeltsin.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the two 1917 revolutions as one event; the February revolution ended the monarchy, while the October revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power. Mistake: equating 'Russia' and 'the Soviet Union'; the USSR (1922-1991) was a federation of republics, of which Russia was the largest. Mistake: confusing Gorbachev's two reforms; perestroika restructured the economy, while glasnost opened public life. Exit: (a) Which revolution of 1917 brought the Bolsheviks to power? (b) When did the Soviet Union dissolve? (c) Name Gorbachev's two signature policies. Answers: the October Revolution; 1991; perestroika and glasnost. With the historical backbone in place, we turn to the language that carried this culture.

questions.explanation: Baikal is the world's deepest and oldest freshwater lake, holding an enormous volume of water.

questions.explanation: Kievan Rus adopted Christianity under Vladimir the Great in 988.

options: founding Saint Petersburg and turning Russia toward Europe
questions.explanation: Peter founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 and modernized Russia along western lines.

questions.explanation: The tsar abdicated in February 1917, and the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917.

questions.explanation: Gagarin became the first person to travel into space in 1961, a Cold War milestone.

lessons.title: The Russian language and Cyrillic
lessons.grammar_note: Russian has no articles ('a' or 'the') and marks grammatical roles with case endings instead of fixed word order.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what kind of language Russian is, where its alphabet came from, and what makes its grammar distinctive. By the end you will be able to describe the Cyrillic script, name the saints traditionally linked to its creation, and recognize a few features that set Russian apart from English, such as grammatical cases and verb aspect. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which alphabet is used to write Russian? You do not need to learn the language itself here; the goal is cultural literacy, so that you understand why Russian looks and sounds the way it does and how it connects to the wider Slavic world. You will also see how the language became a vehicle for one of the richest literary traditions anywhere, which is exactly where the next lesson leads. By the end you should feel comfortable explaining Cyrillic to someone who has never seen it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Russian is an East Slavic language, the most widely spoken of all the Slavic languages, and one of the most spoken languages in the world. It is written in the Cyrillic alphabet, which today has thirty-three letters. Cyrillic developed in the ninth and tenth centuries and is traditionally connected to the Byzantine missionaries Saints Cyril and Methodius, who devised a script to bring Christian texts to the Slavs; the alphabet was later named for Cyril. Russian grammar relies on inflection: nouns, adjectives, and pronouns change their endings across six grammatical cases to show their role in a sentence, which means word order can be flexible. Verbs come in aspect pairs, imperfective for ongoing or repeated actions and perfective for completed ones. There are no articles. These features make the language compact and precise, and they give Russian poetry and prose a music that is hard to carry fully into English.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: The tradition credits Saints Cyril and Methodius, brothers from Thessalonica, with creating a Slavic script in the ninth century; the earlier Glagolitic alphabet is attributed to them directly, while the Cyrillic that bears Cyril's name was developed by their followers and became standard in the Orthodox Slavic world. Over the centuries the alphabet was simplified, most sharply by Peter the Great, who reformed the letterforms in the early eighteenth century to create a cleaner 'civil script,' and again after the 1917 revolution, when several letters were dropped. The language also absorbed waves of borrowing, from Church Slavonic and Greek in religious vocabulary to French during the imperial era and English in modern times. Beyond Russia, Cyrillic serves many other languages, from Ukrainian and Bulgarian to Serbian and Mongolian. The script is thus both a national symbol and a shared inheritance across a broad cultural region.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) To which family of languages does Russian belong? 2) What script is used to write it, and about how many letters does it have? 3) Which two saints are traditionally linked to the Slavic alphabet? 4) How many grammatical cases does Russian use? 5) What are the two verb aspects called? 6) Which ruler reformed the letterforms into a 'civil script' in the early eighteenth century? Answers: 1) The East Slavic branch of the Slavic languages. 2) Cyrillic, with thirty-three letters today. 3) Saints Cyril and Methodius. 4) Six. 5) Imperfective and perfective. 6) Peter the Great.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling Cyrillic a form of the Greek or Latin alphabet; it is its own script, though it drew on Greek letterforms. Mistake: assuming Russian word order must be fixed like English; case endings carry the grammar, so order can shift for emphasis. Mistake: thinking only Russia uses Cyrillic; many languages across eastern Europe and Asia use it too. Exit: (a) What script is Russian written in? (b) Which two saints are traditionally credited with the Slavic alphabet? (c) Name one other language that uses Cyrillic. Answers: Cyrillic; Saints Cyril and Methodius; for example Bulgarian, Serbian, Ukrainian, or Mongolian. With the language in view, we can now enter its celebrated literature.

lessons.title: Literature: the golden age
lessons.grammar_note: Dostoevsky is also spelled Dostoyevsky, and Tolstoy's first name Leo renders the Russian Lev; romanized spellings vary.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the giants of nineteenth-century Russian literature and match each to a major work. By the end you will be able to introduce Pushkin, Gogol, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, and Chekhov, and say in a sentence why each matters. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, who wrote 'War and Peace'? You will learn how, in less than a century, Russian writers moved from founding a national literary language to producing some of the most influential novels, stories, and plays ever written. You do not need to have read these works; the aim is to recognize the names, the titles, and the themes that made Russian literature a world force. You will also see how these writers wrestled with faith, conscience, freedom, and the fate of ordinary people under autocracy, questions that still give their books their power. By the end you should be able to recommend a starting point for a curious reader.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Russian literature flowered in the nineteenth century, often called its golden age. It began with poetry and the shaping of a modern literary language, then turned toward the great realist novel, a form Russian writers brought to extraordinary psychological and moral depth. These authors did not write mere entertainment; they probed the human conscience, the meaning of suffering, the pull between faith and doubt, and the lives of serfs, clerks, and nobles alike. Because open political debate was dangerous under the tsars, literature became the arena where the deepest national questions were argued. The result was a body of work read and studied across the world: sweeping historical novels, intense philosophical dramas, and quiet, precise short stories. The tradition continued into the twentieth century despite censorship, but its towering reputation rests above all on the five figures below, whose books remain fixtures of world classrooms and bookshelves alike.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Alexander Pushkin (1799-1837) is regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature; his verse novel 'Eugene Onegin' set the standard for the national literary language. Nikolai Gogol (1809-1852) blended satire and the grotesque in the novel 'Dead Souls' and the story 'The Overcoat.' Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821-1881) explored guilt, faith, and free will in 'Crime and Punishment' and 'The Brothers Karamazov.' Leo Tolstoy (1828-1910) wrote the epics 'War and Peace,' set against Napoleon's invasion, and 'Anna Karenina,' a tragedy of love and society. Anton Chekhov (1860-1904), a master of the short story and the modern stage, wrote plays such as 'The Seagull' and 'The Cherry Orchard' that changed how theater handles mood and the unspoken. Together these five authors turned Russian fiction into a summit of world literature within a single remarkable century.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who is regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature, and what is his verse novel? 2) Which author wrote 'Dead Souls' and 'The Overcoat'? 3) Name the author of 'Crime and Punishment.' 4) Which two epics did Tolstoy write? 5) Who wrote 'The Cherry Orchard' and is famed for the modern short story and play? 6) Against which war is 'War and Peace' set? Answers: 1) Alexander Pushkin; 'Eugene Onegin.' 2) Nikolai Gogol. 3) Fyodor Dostoevsky. 4) 'War and Peace' and 'Anna Karenina.' 5) Anton Chekhov. 6) Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: crediting 'War and Peace' to Dostoevsky; it is Tolstoy's. Mistake: treating Chekhov only as a short-story writer; he is equally famous as a playwright who reshaped modern drama. Mistake: thinking Pushkin wrote long realist novels; his central achievement is poetry, including the verse novel 'Eugene Onegin.' Exit: (a) Who wrote 'The Brothers Karamazov'? (b) Which author is called the founder of modern Russian literature? (c) Name one Chekhov play. Answers: Fyodor Dostoevsky; Alexander Pushkin; for example 'The Seagull' or 'The Cherry Orchard.' From the written word we move to sound and motion: Russian music and ballet.

lessons.title: Music, ballet, and the visual arts
lessons.grammar_note: The Bolshoi ('big') is in Moscow and the Mariinsky is in Saint Petersburg; the latter was called the Kirov in the Soviet era.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify the leading Russian composers, the two great ballet companies, and the main currents of Russian visual art. By the end you will be able to match composers to famous works, say where the Bolshoi and the Mariinsky are, and describe the icon tradition and the later avant-garde. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, who composed 'Swan Lake' and 'The Nutcracker'? You will learn how Russia became a powerhouse of classical music and dance, exporting ballet and symphonies around the world, and how its painters moved from sacred icons to bold modern abstraction. You do not need musical training; the goal is to recognize the names and works that make Russian performing and visual arts globally famous, and to understand how church, court, and revolution each shaped them. By the end you should be able to suggest a first piece of music, a ballet, and a painting for someone new to Russian art.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In the nineteenth century Russian composers forged a national style, drawing on folk melody and sweeping emotion. A group known as the Mighty Handful, or The Five, promoted a distinctly Russian sound, while others blended it with European training. The result ranges from lush symphonies and operas to the ballet scores that remain concert staples. Ballet itself became a Russian art form of the highest prestige, supported by imperial theaters and later by touring companies that astonished the West. In painting, the oldest tradition is the religious icon, a sacred image governed by strict conventions; in the nineteenth century realist painters turned to everyday Russian life, and in the early twentieth century a daring avant-garde pushed toward pure abstraction. Across music, dance, and canvas, Russian artists repeatedly took forms inherited from church or Europe and remade them into something unmistakably their own, admired on every continent.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Pyotr Tchaikovsky (1840-1893) composed the ballets 'Swan Lake,' 'The Sleeping Beauty,' and 'The Nutcracker,' plus the '1812 Overture.' Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov (1844-1908), a member of The Five, wrote the vivid orchestral suite 'Scheherazade.' Igor Stravinsky (1882-1971) revolutionized music with 'The Firebird' and 'The Rite of Spring,' whose 1913 premiere caused an uproar. Dmitri Shostakovich (1906-1975) composed searing symphonies, including the wartime 'Leningrad' Symphony. In dance, the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow and the Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg are the two historic companies. In painting, the medieval monk Andrei Rublev created icons such as 'The Trinity'; the nineteenth-century realist Ilya Repin painted 'Barge Haulers on the Volga'; and the avant-garde Kazimir Malevich startled the art world with 'Black Square' in 1915.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who composed 'The Nutcracker' and 'Swan Lake'? 2) Which composer wrote 'The Rite of Spring,' premiered in 1913? 3) In which cities are the Bolshoi and Mariinsky theaters? 4) What is the oldest Russian painting tradition, and who created 'The Trinity'? 5) Which composer, a member of The Five, wrote 'Scheherazade'? 6) Who painted 'Black Square' in 1915? Answers: 1) Pyotr Tchaikovsky. 2) Igor Stravinsky. 3) The Bolshoi in Moscow and the Mariinsky in Saint Petersburg. 4) The religious icon; Andrei Rublev. 5) Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. 6) Kazimir Malevich.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: placing both great ballet companies in one city; the Bolshoi is in Moscow and the Mariinsky in Saint Petersburg. Mistake: assuming Russian painting is only sacred icons; realists and a radical avant-garde followed. Mistake: crediting 'The Rite of Spring' to Tchaikovsky; it is Stravinsky's. Exit: (a) Who composed 'The Nutcracker'? (b) Where is the Mariinsky Theatre? (c) Who painted 'Black Square'? Answers: Pyotr Tchaikovsky; Saint Petersburg; Kazimir Malevich. Next we turn to faith, custom, and the rhythm of daily life that surrounds all this art.

lessons.title: Faith, food, daily life, and modern culture

items.translation: the dominant Christian church of Russia, descended from the conversion of 988 and known for its icons and choral liturgy
items.example: The Russian Orthodox Church shaped art, music, and the calendar of feasts for a thousand years.

items.translation: the rounded, pointed dome crowning Orthodox churches, often brightly colored or gilded
items.example: The onion domes of Saint Basil's Cathedral on Red Square were built in the sixteenth century.

items.translation: a sacred painted image of Christ, the Virgin, or a saint, venerated in the Orthodox tradition
items.example: Families kept an icon in a special corner of the home for daily prayer.

items.translation: the most important feast of the Orthodox year, celebrating the resurrection, with midnight services and special foods
items.example: At Pascha people greet one another with 'Christ is risen' and share decorated eggs and sweet bread.

items.translation: a beet-based soup, usually served with a spoonful of sour cream
items.example: A bowl of borscht with dark bread is a classic cold-weather meal.

items.translation: thin pancakes served with sweet or savory toppings, central to the Maslenitsa festival
items.example: During Maslenitsa, families eat blini with butter, jam, or caviar to mark the end of winter.

items.translation: small boiled dumplings filled with seasoned meat
items.example: In Siberia, large batches of pelmeni were frozen outdoors to store through the winter.

items.translation: a metal urn for heating water, the traditional heart of Russian tea drinking
items.example: Guests gathered around the samovar for strong tea and long conversation.

items.translation: the Russian steam bathhouse, a social and cleansing ritual
items.example: A visit to the banya, followed by a plunge into cold water, is a cherished weekly custom.

items.translation: a country cottage where city families spend summers and grow vegetables
items.example: Many Muscovites escape to the dacha on summer weekends to garden and relax.

items.translation: a set of nested wooden dolls, a well-known Russian folk craft and souvenir
items.example: Each matryoshka opens to reveal a smaller doll painted inside.

items.translation: a Russian or Soviet space traveler; the Soviet program achieved the first human spaceflight in 1961
items.example: Yuri Gagarin, the first cosmonaut in orbit, became a national hero.

lessons.title: Checkpoint 2: language, arts, faith, and life

questions.prompt: Russian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet, traditionally linked to...
questions.explanation: The Slavic script is traditionally credited to the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius in the ninth century.

questions.prompt: Which author wrote both 'Crime and Punishment' and 'The Brothers Karamazov'?
questions.explanation: Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821-1881) wrote both novels of conscience and faith.

questions.prompt: The Bolshoi and the Mariinsky are famous Russian institutions of...
questions.explanation: The Bolshoi in Moscow and the Mariinsky in Saint Petersburg are the two historic ballet and opera theaters.

questions.prompt: Igor Stravinsky is best known for the groundbreaking 1913 work...
questions.explanation: 'The Rite of Spring' caused a famous uproar at its 1913 premiere.

questions.prompt: The onion domes and icon painting of Russia belong above all to the tradition of...

questions.explanation: Borscht is the beet-based soup; pelmeni are dumplings, blini are pancakes, and a samovar heats tea water.
